div.head: Hn 80.3a
div.ab: Et uia regia dicitur que semper aperta est, quam nemo conclaudere potest uel auertere [ter]minis suis, que ducit in ciuitatem uel burgum uel castrum uel portum (regium).
div.note: New row (October 2026): Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 596 (two independent readings of the page images, differences settled against the page)

note.seg: abwenden durch private Grenzmarken der Besiedlung; vgl. 80, 5a; das Wort vielleicht aus Isa. 58, 12: auertens semitas in quietem. Eine Freibürgschaftsjury rügt 1290 bounds removed and the king’s highway straitened; Maitland Sel. pleas man. 162

divert by private boundary marks of settlement; cf. 80, 5a; the word perhaps from Isa. 58, 12: auertens semitas in quietem. In 1290 a frankpledge jury presents bounds removed and the king’s highway straitened; Maitland Sel. pleas man. 162

cum statt ter- lesen, da Archetyp ē und t' kaum unterschied, Hss. Edd. [Hn setzt aber nicht cum statt Abl. instrum.]; dahinter liest minis, verb. aus muris Sc; nimis Hg; ruinis Sl; ramis K Co Tw; pannis Or Gi. Ohne jene Silbe ginge muris, das Pollock Oxford lect. 82 vermuthete: Heinrich I. erlaubt S. Trinity zu London, ut claudant muro uiam (ed. Sharpe Cal. of letter-books of London C p. 75); und 1221 rügt eine Jury, quod leuauit murum super uiam; Maitland Pleas of Gloucester n. 68

MSS and Edd. read cum instead of ter-, since the archetype hardly distinguished ē from t’ [but Hn does not use cum in place of the instrumental abl.]; after it Sc reads minis, corrected from muris; nimis Hg; ruinis Sl; ramis K Co Tw; pannis Or Gi. Without that syllable, muris, which Pollock Oxford lect. 82 conjectured, would be possible: Henry I permits S. Trinity at London ut claudant muro uiam (ed. Sharpe Cal. of letter-books of London C p. 75); and in 1221 a jury presents quod leuauit murum super uiam; Maitland Pleas of Gloucester n. 68
vgl. Très anc. cout. Norm. II 70: uia regia que ducit a ciuitate in ciuitatem uel castellum regium
cf. Très anc. cout. Norm. II 70: uia regia que ducit a ciuitate in ciuitatem uel castellum regium
thus Sc Hg; claudere the others

minis schreibend dachte Kopist wohl an ‘Gräben, Erdarbeiten’; doch ist dies nur für ‘unterminieren’ seit 14. Jh. belegt (Ducange, Godefroy, La Curne St. Palaye; vgt. 80, 5 fodiendo); zur muris-Lesart vgl. die Anm.f und die Bed. ‘Erdwall mit Graswuchs’ 1290 zu Norwich (Hudson Leet in Norwich 37); die Lesung ruinis erklärte Pollock (Law Quart. Rev. I [1885] 46): ‘rubbish’; die Variante ramis stützt sich auf arborem deicere im Gl Strasse 9.—Ich verstehe terminis ‘Grenzsteine, Ackerschranken’; vgl. das Bepflügen der Landstrasse ebd. 9c.—Wünscht man die Strasse, die um einen Ort herumlief, in ihn hinein verlegt, so bedarf das königlicher Gnade; so für Caen a. 1077; Round Cal. of docum. France n. 449

In writing minis the copyist was probably thinking of ‘ditches, earthworks’; but this is attested only in the sense ‘undermine’, and only from the 14th cent. (Ducange, Godefroy, La Curne St. Palaye; cf. 80, 5 fodiendo); on the reading muris cf. note f and the meaning ‘earthen bank overgrown with grass’ in 1290 at Norwich (Hudson Leet in Norwich 37); the reading ruinis was explained by Pollock (Law Quart. Rev. I [1885] 46) as ‘rubbish’; the variant ramis rests on arborem deicere in Gl Strasse 9.—I take terminis as ‘boundary stones, field barriers’; cf. the ploughing up of the highway ibid. 9c.—If it was desired that a road running round a place be moved into it, this required the king’s grace; thus for Caen in 1077; Round Cal. of docum. France n. 449
Vgl.: de civitate ad civitatem im Gl Strasse 9, und in Urk. a. 1074 über Strasse de mercato ad mercatum et de portu maris ad alium portum Birch Domesday 295.—regium{20} Rs
